lead: A refrigerator does not create cold; it moves heat from a cold space to a warmer one, and that costs work. The same cycle used for the heat it rejects is a heat pump. Kitchen refrigerators, air conditioners, cold stores and vaccine storage all use the vapour-compression cycle, and gas liquefaction pushes the same idea to very low temperatures.
prereq: You need: the device balances of heat engines, refrigerators and heat pumps, the Carnot COP from the Carnot cycle, and refrigerant property tables (thermodynamic property tables and diagrams).

sections.h3: The four devices of the vapour-compression cycle

blocks.text: Refrigeration keeps a space colder than its surroundings. Heat leaks in, so a device must continuously pump that heat to a warmer place. The vapour-compression cycle does this by making a fluid boil at low pressure, absorbing heat, and condense at high pressure, releasing heat.

A liquid boils at a temperature fixed by its pressure. Lower the pressure, and the boiling point falls. Pick a refrigerant whose boiling point at a few atmospheres is below the cold-space temperature; the cold space then supplies the heat of boiling. The cycle runs in four steps.

items: Evaporator. A low-pressure liquid–vapour mixture boils at constant pressure and temperature, taking heat Qin from the cold space.
Compressor. Low-pressure vapour is squeezed to high pressure. Work W<sub>in</sub> goes in, so the vapour leaves superheated and hotter.
Condenser. Hot high-pressure vapour gives heat Q<sub>out</sub> to surroundings and condenses to liquid.

Expansion valve (throttle). Liquid drops to low pressure through a restriction. No work is produced, enthalpy stays nearly constant, temperature falls, and a little liquid flashes to vapour. The cold mixture returns to the evaporator.

blocks.text: For steady flow, neglecting kinetic and potential energy, Q<sub>in</sub> + W<sub>in</sub> = Q<sub>out</sub>. The condenser duty is always larger than the refrigerating effect by the compressor work.

sections.h3: Coefficient of performance and the Carnot limit

blocks.text: Efficiency is a poor word for a refrigerator, because we want heat removed, not work. The yardstick is the coefficient of performance (COP).

blocks.where: COP<sub>R</sub> is the coefficient of performance of the refrigerator (dimensionless); Q<sub>in</sub> is the heat taken from the cold space in kW; Q<sub>out</sub> is the heat rejected at the condenser in kW; W<sub>in</sub> is the compressor work in kW.
COP<sub>HP</sub> is the heat-pump COP; Q<sub>out</sub> is heat delivered to the warm room in kW. COP<sub>HP</sub> = COP<sub>R</sub> + 1 because the work also ends up in the room.

blocks.text: No cycle between cold at T<sub>C</sub> and warm at T<sub>H</sub> can beat the reversed Carnot cycle. Its COP depends only on the two absolute temperatures.

blocks.where: T<sub>C</sub> is cold-region temperature in kelvin; T<sub>H</sub> is warm-region temperature in kelvin. Use kelvin, never Celsius, because the ratio must stay positive and correct.

blocks.text: Real machines reach roughly half the Carnot value: compression is not isentropic, the throttle wastes pressure energy, and heat exchangers need a finite temperature difference. That gap is destroyed work, as in lost work and ideal work.

sections.h3: Real cycles, Joule–Thomson expansion and liquefaction

blocks.text: The ideal cycle assumes saturated vapour entering the compressor and saturated liquid leaving the condenser. Practical cycles differ:

items: The vapour is superheated a few degrees before compression. Liquid droplets damage a compressor, and superheat guarantees dry vapour.
The condensate is subcooled, raising refrigerating effect per kilogram.
Compression is not isentropic; isentropic efficiency is typically 0.7 to 0.85. Use the actual compressor exit enthalpy, not the isentropic one.

blocks.text: The expansion valve is a throttling device: enthalpy is constant across it and entropy rises, so it is irreversible. For most gases below their inversion temperature, throttling also lowers temperature. This is the Joule–Thomson effect, and it makes gas liquefaction possible without moving cold parts.
Liquefaction needs cooling below the critical temperature of the gas, above which no pressure can condense the vapour (126 K for nitrogen). The two classic cycles are:

items: Linde cycle. Compress the gas at room temperature, cool it in a counter-current heat exchanger, and throttle it. Part of the gas liquefies; the cold gas left over returns through the exchanger to pre-cool the incoming stream. With a perfect exchanger the liquid fraction is y = (h₁ − h₂)/(h₁ − hf), where h₁ is the low-pressure gas at room temperature, h₂ the high-pressure gas at room temperature and hf the saturated liquid.
Claude cycle. Adds an expansion engine, so part of the gas expands while doing work. Work removal gives far more cooling per kilogram, so Claude suits large tonnages.

examples.question: An ideal vapour-compression refrigerator uses R-134a between 0.14 MPa and 0.8 MPa, with a flow of 0.05 kg/s. Table values: saturated vapour at 0.14 MPa (−18.8 °C), h₁ = 387.3 kJ/kg, s₁ = 1.7402 kJ/(kg·K); at 0.8 MPa and s = 1.7402, h₂ = 423.5 kJ/kg (39.0 °C); saturated liquid at 0.8 MPa (31.3 °C), h₃ = 243.6 kJ/kg. Find the refrigerating effect, compressor power, condenser duty, COP, and compare with the Carnot COP between −18.8 °C and 31.3 °C.
steps: Throttle: h₄ = h₃ = 243.6 kJ/kg (the mixture entering the evaporator has quality 0.32).
Refrigerating effect: Q<sub>in</sub> = ṁ(h₁ − h₄) = 0.05 × (387.3 − 243.6) = 0.05 × 143.7 = 7.18 kW.
Condenser: Q<sub>out</sub> = ṁ(h₂ − h₃) = 0.05 × 179.9 = 9.00 kW = Q<sub>in</sub> + W<sub>in</sub>.

Carnot: T<sub>C</sub> = 254.4 K, T<sub>H</sub> = 304.5 K, so COP = 254.4/50.1 = 5.08. The ideal vapour cycle reaches 3.97/5.08 = 0.78 of it; the throttle and the superheated discharge account for the gap.
examples.answer: Q<sub>in</sub> = 7.18 kW, W<sub>in</sub> = 1.81 kW, Q<sub>out</sub> = 9.00 kW, COP<sub>R</sub> = 3.97 against a Carnot COP of 5.08.

examples.question: A Linde plant compresses nitrogen to 200 bar at 300 K and returns the unliquefied gas at 1 atm and 300 K. From a nitrogen table: h₁ − h₂ = 32.1 kJ/kg (gas at 1 atm and 300 K minus gas at 200 bar and 300 K) and h₁ − h<sub>f</sub> = 433.2 kJ/kg (h<sub>f</sub> is saturated liquid at 1 atm, 77 K). Find the fraction liquefied and the liquid made per 100 kg of gas compressed.
steps: Energy balance on the cold box (exchanger, valve and separator, adiabatic, no work): ṁh₂ = y ṁ h<sub>f</sub> + (1 − y) ṁ h₁.
Per 100 kg compressed: 7.4 kg of liquid nitrogen; 92.6 kg goes back to the compressor.
h₂ < h₁ at the same 300 K means nitrogen cools on throttling at room temperature (positive Joule–Thomson coefficient), so the simple Linde cycle works for it.
examples.answer: y = 0.074: about 7.4 kg of liquid per 100 kg of nitrogen compressed.

traps: Putting Celsius into COP = T<sub>C</sub>/(T<sub>H</sub> − T<sub>C</sub>). For −23 °C and 27 °C the right answer is 250/50 = 5; Celsius gives −23/50 = −0.46, which is nonsense. The difference survives either scale, the numerator does not.
Forgetting COP<sub>HP</sub> = COP<sub>R</sub> + 1; a heat pump shows a larger number than the refrigerator it is built from.
Treating the expansion valve as a turbine. It is a throttle: h is constant, no work, and entropy rises.
Using the isentropic compressor exit enthalpy when an isentropic efficiency is given; the real exit has h₂ = h₁ + (h₂s − h₁)/η<sub>c</sub>, higher than h₂s.
Writing evaporator heat as Q<sub>out</sub>. The evaporator takes heat in; the condenser rejects heat out.

quiz.q: Define the coefficient of performance of a refrigerator and state the formula.
quiz.a: COP<sub>R</sub> = Q<sub>in</sub> / W<sub>in</sub>, where Q<sub>in</sub> is the heat removed from the cold space in kW and W<sub>in</sub> is the compressor work in kW. It is dimensionless.

quiz.q: Why does the expansion valve produce no work even though the pressure falls a lot?
quiz.a: The flow passes through a narrow restriction with no moving part and little kinetic-energy change, so no shaft work crosses the boundary. It is a throttling process with constant enthalpy; pressure energy appears as increased entropy, not work.

quiz.q: A refrigerator works between 260 K and 305 K, removes 4 kW, and has an actual COP of 2.0. Find the compressor work and the Carnot COP.
quiz.a: W<sub>in</sub> = Q<sub>in</sub>/COP<sub>R</sub> = 4/2.0 = 2 kW. COP<sub>Carnot</sub> = 260/(305 − 260) = 260/45 = 5.78. The real machine reaches 2.0/5.78 = 0.35 of the limit.

quiz.q: A heat pump delivers 12 kW to a room and has COP<sub>HP</sub> = 4. Find the compressor work and the COP of the same unit working as a refrigerator.
quiz.a: W<sub>in</sub> = Q<sub>out</sub>/COP<sub>HP</sub> = 12/4 = 3 kW. Q<sub>in</sub> = Q<sub>out</sub> − W<sub>in</sub> = 12 − 3 = 9 kW, so COP<sub>R</sub> = 9/3 = 3 = COP<sub>HP</sub> − 1.

quiz.q: Why must the vapour leaving the evaporator be superheated before it enters the compressor?
quiz.a: Liquid drops entering a compressor can break its valves, because liquid hardly compresses. A few kelvin of superheat at the evaporator exit makes sure only dry vapour enters. A thermostatic expansion valve senses that superheat and feeds just enough refrigerant to boil off before the end of the coil.

quiz.q: State in one line each how the Linde and Claude liquefaction cycles differ.
quiz.a: Linde uses only a Joule–Thomson throttle after a counter-current heat exchanger; Claude adds an expansion engine that removes work, giving more cooling per unit mass.

beyond: Not for the exam. Plants moved away from ozone-depleting refrigerants, so ammonia, CO₂ and hydrocarbons are back; absorption chillers replace the compressor with waste heat. Search for "cascade refrigeration", "absorption chiller" and "Joule–Thomson inversion temperature of hydrogen".
